steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on MaskDiT, which speeds up diffusion model training by masking patches in a transformer backbone. Motivate the training cost problem, explain why masked training doesn't fit U-Nets but does fit DiT, describe our method and headline ImageNet results, and list contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Diffusion models: popularity, applications, training cost bottleneck
2. Masked training in representation learning
3. Why masked training does not fit U-Net
4. Transformer backbones for diffusion (DiT)
5. Our hypothesis and MaskDiT design
6. Results on ImageNet
7. Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Diffusion models
- most popular deep generative models; superior image generation; text-to-image
- applications: image-to-image translation, personalized creation, model robustness
- large-scale training essential, but costly in compute/time -> bottleneck
- original stable diffusion: 256 A100 GPUs, >24 days; improved infra: 13 days on 256 A100
- still inaccessible to most; efficiency an open question

2. Masked training
- used in NLP, computer vision, vision-language understanding
- cuts training time and memory, esp. in vision
- self-supervised, no loss of representation quality (visual redundancy, learn from unmasked patches)
- relies on transformers: operate on patches, natural to mask

3. U-Net problem
- diffusion models mostly U-Net backbone with modifications
- convolutions on regular dense grids -> hard to use masked tokens / random patch subsets

4. Transformer backbones
- replacing U-Net with ViT: similar or better on standard benchmarks
- DiT: ViT best practices, no U-Net inductive bias, scalable
- DiT training expensive (millions of iterations) -> opportunity for efficient training

5. MaskDiT
- hypothesis: significant redundancy in pixel space -> DSM loss on subset of pixels
- advantages: smaller input per iteration; multiple views as augmentation (limited data)
- asymmetric encoder-decoder: encoder on unmasked patches, lightweight decoder on all patches
- objective: DSM score of unmasked patches + MSE reconstruction of masked patches (global knowledge, avoids overfitting)
- same masking ratio (e.g., 50%) for all timesteps
- finetune without masking afterwards; <6% of total cost

6. Results
- 50% patches removed -> 2\times cheaper per iteration; fewer steps to match DiT
- ImageNet-256 \times 256: FID 5.69 w/o guidance (beats non-cascaded), 2.28 with guidance
- 273 hours on 8 \times A100, 31% of DiT's time
- ImageNet-512 \times 512: FID 10.79 / 2.50; beats DiT-XL/2; 209 A100 GPU days, ~29% of DiT-XL/2

7. Contributions
- fast training with masked transformers, masking 50% of patches
- asymmetric encoder-decoder + new objective
- faster, less memory, comparable quality; scalability

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Diffusion models are now the most popular class of deep generative models, because they have superior image generation performance, especially when synthesizing high-quality and diverse images from text inputs. Because they generate so well, they have enabled many applications, including image-to-image translation, personalized creation and model robustness. Training these models at large scale is essential for them to generate realistic images and creative art. But training them needs a lot of computational resources and time, and this is still a major bottleneck for scaling them up further. For example, the original stable diffusion was trained on 256 A100 GPUs for more than 24 days. With better infrastructure and implementation the training cost can be brought down to 13 days on 256 A100 GPUs, but this is still not accessible to most researchers and practitioners. So improving the training efficiency of diffusion models is still an open question.

In representation learning, masked training is used a lot to improve training efficiency, in domains like natural language processing, computer vision, and vision-language understanding. Masked training reduces the overall training time and memory significantly, especially in vision applications. Masked training is also an effective self-supervised learning technique that does not hurt the quality of representation learning, since there is high redundancy in visual appearance and so the model can learn from the unmasked patches. Masked training depends heavily on the transformer architecture, because transformers operate on patches and it is natural to mask some of them.

However, masked training can't be applied directly to diffusion models, because current diffusion models mostly use U-Net as the standard network backbone, with some modifications. The convolutions in U-Net work on regular dense grids, so it is hard to incorporate masked tokens and to train with a random subset of the input patches. So it is not straightforward to apply masked training to U-Net models.

4. Transformer backbones for diffusion
- ViT instead of U-Net: similar or better on benchmarks
- DiT: ViT best practices, no U-Net inductive bias, scalable; but expensive (millions of iterations)

5. MaskDiT
- hypothesis: pixel-space redundancy -> DSM loss on a subset of pixels
- advantages: cheaper iterations; multiple views as augmentation
- asymmetric encoder-decoder; DSM on unmasked + MSE reconstruction of masked patches
- same masking ratio (e.g., 50%) for all timesteps; finetune without masking, <6% of cost

6. Results
- 2\times cheaper per iteration
- ImageNet-256 \times 256: FID 5.69 / 2.28; 273 hours on 8 \times A100, 31% of DiT
- ImageNet-512 \times 512: FID 10.79 / 2.50; 209 A100 GPU days, ~29% of DiT-XL/2

7. Contributions: masked transformers for fast training; encoder-decoder + new objective; faster, less memory, scalable

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Diffusion models are now the most popular class of deep generative models, because they have superior image generation performance, especially when synthesizing high-quality and diverse images from text inputs. Because they generate so well, they have enabled many applications, including image-to-image translation, personalized creation and model robustness. Training these models at large scale is essential for them to generate realistic images and creative art. But training them needs a lot of computational resources and time, and this is still a major bottleneck for scaling them up further. For example, the original stable diffusion was trained on 256 A100 GPUs for more than 24 days. With better infrastructure and implementation the training cost can be brought down to 13 days on 256 A100 GPUs, but this is still not accessible to most researchers and practitioners. So improving the training efficiency of diffusion models is still an open question.

In representation learning, masked training is used a lot to improve training efficiency, in domains like natural language processing, computer vision, and vision-language understanding. Masked training reduces the overall training time and memory significantly, especially in vision applications. Masked training is also an effective self-supervised learning technique that does not hurt the quality of representation learning, since there is high redundancy in visual appearance and so the model can learn from the unmasked patches. Masked training depends heavily on the transformer architecture, because transformers operate on patches and it is natural to mask some of them.

However, masked training can't be applied directly to diffusion models, because current diffusion models mostly use U-Net as the standard network backbone, with some modifications. The convolutions in U-Net work on regular dense grids, so it is hard to incorporate masked tokens and to train with a random subset of the input patches. So it is not straightforward to apply masked training to U-Net models.

Recently a few works showed that if you replace the U-Net architecture with vision transformers (ViT) as the backbone of diffusion models, you can get similar or even better performance on standard image generation benchmarks. In particular, Diffusion Transformer (DiT) inherits the best practices of ViTs and doesn't rely on the U-Net inductive bias, which shows that the DiT backbone is scalable for diffusion models. Like standard ViTs, DiTs are computationally expensive to train and need millions of iterations. But this also opens new opportunities for training large transformer-based diffusion models efficiently.

In this work we use the transformer structure of DiTs to do masked modeling, so that training is much faster and cheaper. Our main hypothesis is that images have a lot of redundancy in pixel space. So it should be possible to train diffusion models by minimizing the denoising score matching (DSM) loss on only a subset of pixels. Masked training has two main advantages: 1) we only need to pass a small subset of image patches to the network, which reduces the computational cost per iteration a lot. 2) we can augment the training data with multiple views, which can improve training performance, especially when data is limited.

Based on this hypothesis, we propose an efficient approach for training large transformer-based diffusion models, which we call Masked Diffusion Transformer (MaskDiT). First we use an asymmetric encoder-decoder architecture: the transformer encoder only operates on the unmasked patches, and a lightweight transformer decoder operates on all the patches. Then we design a new training objective with two parts: 1) predicting the score of the unmasked patches with the DSM loss, and 2) reconstructing the masked patches of the input with the mean square error (MSE) loss. The second part gives global knowledge of the whole image, which stops the diffusion model from overfitting to the unmasked patches. To keep it simple, we use the same masking ratio (e.g., 50%) for all the diffusion timesteps in training. After training, we finetune the model without masking to close the distribution gap between training and inference, and this only adds a minimal overhead (less than 6% of the total training cost).

Because we randomly remove 50% of the patches of training images, our method reduces the training cost per iteration by 2\times. With the new architecture and the new training objective, MaskDiT can also reach similar performance to DiT with fewer training steps, so the overall training cost is much smaller. On the class-conditional ImageNet-256 \times 256 generation benchmark, MaskDiT gets an FID of 5.69 without guidance, which is better than previous (non-cascaded) diffusion models, and an FID of 2.28 with guidance, which is comparable to the state-of-the-art models. The total training cost of MaskDiT to reach FID 2.28 is 273 hours on 8 \times A100 GPUs, which is only 31% of DiT's training time. On class-conditional ImageNet-512 \times 512, MaskDiT gets an FID of 10.79 without guidance and 2.50 with guidance, which is better than DiT-XL/2 and prior diffusion models. The total training cost is 209 A100 GPU days, about 29% of the cost of DiT-XL/2, which validates that MaskDiT is scalable and effective. All these results show that our method has significantly better training efficiency in wall-clock time.

Our main contributions are:

- We propose a new approach for fast training of diffusion models with masked transformers, where a high proportion (50%) of input patches is randomly masked out.
- For masked training, we introduce an asymmetric encoder-decoder architecture and a new training objective that predicts the score of the unmasked patches and reconstructs the masked patches.
- We show that our method trains faster and uses less memory while getting comparable generation performance, which implies it can scale to large diffusion models.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Diffusion models [2,3,4] have become the most popular class of deep generative models due to their superior image generation performance [5], particularly in synthesizing high-quality and diverse images from text inputs [6,7,8,9]. Their strong generation performance has enabled many applications, including image-to-image translation [10,11], personalized creation [12,13] and model robustness [14,15]. Large-scale training of these models is essential for generating realistic images and creative art. However, training them requires a large amount of computational resources and time, which remains a major bottleneck for scaling them up further. For example, the original stable diffusion [7] was trained on 256 A100 GPUs for more than 24 days. Although improved infrastructure and implementation can reduce the training cost to 13 days on 256 A100 GPUs [16], this is still inaccessible to most researchers and practitioners. Improving the training efficiency of diffusion models therefore remains an open question.

In the representation learning community, masked training is widely used to improve training efficiency in domains such as natural language processing [17], computer vision [18], and vision-language understanding [19]. Masked training significantly reduces overall training time and memory, especially in vision applications [18,19]. It is also an effective self-supervised learning technique that does not sacrifice representation learning quality, since the high redundancy in visual appearance allows the model to learn from unmasked patches. Masked training relies heavily on the transformer architecture [20], because transformers operate on patches and it is natural to mask a subset of them.

Masked training, however, cannot be directly applied to diffusion models, since current diffusion models mostly use U-Net [21] as the standard network backbone, with some modifications [3,4,5]. The convolutions in U-Net operate on regular dense grids, which makes it challenging to incorporate masked tokens and train with a random subset of the input patches. Applying masked training techniques to U-Net models is therefore not straightforward.

Recently, a few works [1,22] have shown that replacing the U-Net architecture with vision transformers (ViT) [23] as the backbone of diffusion models achieves similar or even better performance on standard image generation benchmarks. In particular, Diffusion Transformer (DiT) [1] inherits the best practices of ViTs without relying on the U-Net inductive bias, demonstrating the scalability of the DiT backbone for diffusion models. As with standard ViTs, training DiTs is computationally expensive and requires millions of iterations. However, this opens up new opportunities for efficient training of large transformer-based diffusion models.

In this work, we leverage the transformer structure of DiTs to enable masked modeling for much faster and cheaper training. Our main hypothesis is that images contain significant redundancy in pixel space, so it is possible to train diffusion models by minimizing the denoising score matching (DSM) loss on only a subset of pixels. Masked training has two main advantages: 1) only a small subset of image patches is passed to the network, which greatly reduces the computational cost per iteration; 2) the training data can be augmented with multiple views, which can improve training performance, particularly in limited-data settings.

Driven by this hypothesis, we propose an efficient approach to training large transformer-based diffusion models, called Masked Diffusion Transformer (MaskDiT). We first adopt an asymmetric encoder-decoder architecture, in which the transformer encoder operates only on the unmasked patches and a lightweight transformer decoder operates on the complete set of patches. We then design a new training objective with two parts: 1) predicting the score of unmasked patches via the DSM loss, and 2) reconstructing the masked patches of the input via the mean square error (MSE) loss. The reconstruction term provides global knowledge of the complete image and prevents the diffusion model from overfitting to the unmasked patches. For simplicity, we apply the same masking ratio (e.g., 50%) across all diffusion timesteps during training. After training, we finetune the model without masking to close the distribution gap between training and inference, which incurs only minimal overhead (less than 6% of the total training cost).

By randomly removing 50% of the patches of training images, our method reduces the per-iteration training cost by 2\times. With the new architecture and training objective, MaskDiT also reaches performance similar to DiT with fewer training steps, leading to much smaller overall training costs. On the class-conditional ImageNet-256 \times 256 generation benchmark, MaskDiT achieves an FID of 5.69 without guidance, outperforming previous (non-cascaded) diffusion models, and an FID of 2.28 with guidance, comparable to state-of-the-art models. To reach FID 2.28, the total training cost of MaskDiT is 273 hours on 8 \times A100 GPUs, only 31% of DiT's training time. On class-conditional ImageNet-512 \times 512, MaskDiT achieves an FID of 10.79 without guidance and 2.50 with guidance, outperforming DiT-XL/2 and prior diffusion models, at a total training cost of 209 A100 GPU days, about 29% of that of DiT-XL/2. This validates the scalability and effectiveness of MaskDiT. Together, these results show that our method offers significantly better training efficiency in wall-clock time.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

- We propose a new approach for fast training of diffusion models with masked transformers that randomly masks out a high proportion (50%) of input patches.
- For masked training, we introduce an asymmetric encoder-decoder architecture and a new training objective that predicts the score of unmasked patches and reconstructs masked patches.
- We show that our method trains faster with less memory while achieving comparable generation performance, implying its scalability to large diffusion models.
